title: Write/Sign for a variety of different purposes

lessons.title: Writing for work: notes, records and forms
lessons.html:
Why we write at work

In a stable yard, many people look after the same horses. The morning groom must tell the afternoon groom what happened. We do this by writing. Writing also gives proof: who did what, and when.

Things you may write

  • A daily stable record: which horses ate, drank, worked, and anything unusual
  • A note to the next shift
  • A message for your supervisor
  • Forms: leave forms, incident reports, stock sheets
  • A list: feed or tack that is running low

Filling in a form

  1. Read the whole form first.
  2. Use a pen, not a pencil. Use capital letters if the form asks for them.
  3. Fill in every box. If a box does not apply, write N/A (not applicable).
  4. Write the date and the time.
  5. Sign your name.
  6. Check before you hand it in.

Writing a daily record

DateHorseAteNotesGroom
12/03DukeAllLunged 20 minT. Mokoena
12/03BellaHalfQuiet, told supervisor 16:00T. Mokoena

Short notes are fine. Write facts: what you saw. Do not write guesses as facts. "Bella left half her feed" is a fact. "Bella is sick" is a guess. Let the supervisor or vet decide.

Example

At 15:00 Peter sees that the grey mare has a small cut on her knee. He writes in the record: date, time, horse, "small cut on left knee, cleaned with water", and his name. He also tells his supervisor before he goes home.

Good handwriting

Write so others can read it. Leave spaces between words. Write numbers clearly; a badly written 1 can look like a 7. In feed and medicine records this can be dangerous.

lessons.title: Writing messages, letters and signing
lessons.html:
Writing a short message

A message must answer: who is it for, what happened or what must be done, and who wrote it.

Example note:

To: Afternoon groom. Date: 14 May, 11:30. Farrier put new front shoes on Storm. Keep him in his stable today. From: Sipho.

Writing a simple letter or request

Sometimes you write to ask for leave or to explain something.

  1. Your name and the date at the top.
  2. Who the letter is for: "Dear Mr Venter".
  3. Say why you are writing in the first sentence: "I would like to ask for leave on 3 and 4 June."
  4. Give the reason and details in one or two sentences.
  5. End politely: "Thank you. Yours faithfully," then your name and signature.

Planning your writing

  • Think: Who will read this? What do they need to know?
  • Write: Use short sentences and simple words.
  • Check: Read it again. Is it clear? Is anything missing? Fix spelling of names and numbers.

Writing for different readers

A note to a co-worker can be short and friendly. A letter to the manager or a report for the vet must be neat and polite. A form must follow the boxes exactly.

Your signature

Your signature means: "I agree" or "I did this." Never sign something you have not read or do not understand. Ask someone to explain it first. Never sign for someone else.

Sign language

Deaf people in South Africa use South African Sign Language. In this unit, "signing" can also mean communicating a message in sign language. The same rules apply: plan the message, make it clear, check it was understood.

Using a phone

WhatsApp messages at work must also be clear and polite. Write the horse's name and the stable number. Do not send rude jokes in work groups.

Key points

  • Write facts, not guesses, in records.
  • Fill in every box on a form, with date, time and signature.
  • A message says who it is for, what must be done and who wrote it.
  • Think, write, check before you hand in.
  • Never sign something you have not read.
